title: Descrybe's Quest to Democratize Legal Research (Kara Peterson & Richard DiBona)
author: Kara Peterson · Richard DiBona

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source contains only podcast closing remarks and no substantive claims about pragmatic AI adoption, experimentation, transformation evidence, leadership, workflows or benchmarks. There is therefore insufficient evidence to determine its position relative to the cluster.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that dependable legal AI requires more than general model capability. It identifies authoritative source material and legal-specific design as important differentiators, while treating displacement by general-purpose providers as a serious but uncertain prospect. Its claims are asserted rather than supported by a disclosed comparative test.
qs: What the big difference is, and this is why we ran the test, is what these models are trained on.
So by the very nature of the way these tools are built right now, they're not particularly good at this authoritative type stuff.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Descrybe supports the proposition that a legal-specific layer can preserve specialist value as general models improve. It attributes differentiation to a curated legal corpus, retrieval architecture and sustained data preparation rather than model knowledge alone, while reported confident errors reinforce the need for authoritative grounding and scrutiny. Its performance advantage remains an inadequately documented founder claim, and it provides limited evidence on lawyer verification or lawyer–engineer workflow design.
qs: Because again, it's not using just model knowledge.
It's using our legal corpus and our training of it.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source supports selective, verification-centred adoption by reporting confident errors across models and warning that lawyers may struggle to distinguish accurate output from fiction. Its claim that a specialised legal corpus improves performance also aligns with the cluster’s view that results vary by tool and infrastructure, though the excerpt provides no methods or numerical results.
qs: And if you imagine someone using that, and this is why I have kind of worry about practicing attorneys using these tools right now because it's very hard to separate the truth from the fiction.
It's using our legal corpus and our training of it.

st.t: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
st.an: The source supports the proposition through Percipient’s claim that outsourced, technology-enabled subpoena work frees corporate teams for core work. Descrybe also portrays AI as amplifying experienced developers’ capacity, although this is qualitative and does not demonstrate measured legal-workload relief or strategic gains.
qs: Basically, Percipient handles legwork so your team can focus on the core work.
But it's like putting on a rocket pack or a jet pack for somebody who already knows what they're doing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Descrybe supports the cluster’s core claim that legal-AI capability is uneven and unsafe to treat as general legal competence. Its reported benchmark found high, variable failure rates and persuasive errors, reinforcing the need for task-specific evaluation, specialized legal data and careful human verification. Its claims about Descrybe’s superior performance are self-reported and do not materially extend the cluster’s broader operating-model proposition.
qs: So overall, the failure rate was high if you look at it.
And if you imagine someone using that, and this is why I have kind of worry about practicing attorneys using these tools right now because it's very hard to separate the truth from the fiction.

kp.k: Personal research barriers motivate an access-to-justice product
kp.d: The founders trace Descrybe to DiBona's employment issue around 2021, when searching Google Scholar and reading lengthy opinions proved difficult and repeated lawyer consultations were unaffordable. Peterson interprets their experience as a systemic access problem, particularly for people with fewer resources. They report launching free search in July 2023; the account establishes their motivation rather than demonstrated improvements in legal outcomes.
qs: Because it's like three weeks between when you're talking to your lawyer and you can't afford to call them every day and ask them every question.
So you can just imagine how much harder it is for people who have less privilege.
So 2023 was when we actually launched this free search in July 2023.

kp.k: AI amplifies an experienced developer's output
kp.d: DiBona describes AI as an accelerator of existing engineering expertise rather than a substitute for knowing how to build systems. He estimates his output as equivalent to 10 programmers while running multiple machines. This is a founder's self-assessment, not a measured productivity study. The founders say their complementary engineering and marketing skills help sustain an intentionally unfunded, two-person company.
qs: So we're a two-person company and we're not funded. And that is all on purpose.
But it's like putting on a rocket pack or a jet pack for somebody who already knows what they're doing.
So I could get done like the equivalent of like 10 programmers now.

kp.k: Scaling still requires human support and specialist help
kp.d: Despite AI-enabled development capacity, the founders report needing programming, marketing, bookkeeping and customer-support assistance. DiBona explicitly resists delegating personal customer support entirely to AI, identifying a service preference that constrains automation and scalability.
qs: we like to do personal customer support and answer everybody directly.
So that's not completely scalable, but we don't want to just give that off to AI because that's not our company vibe.
And of course, I can always use somebody who could program to do stuff.

kp.k: Lower-priced research targets underserved professional buyers
kp.d: Peterson positions Descrybe primarily for solo and small firms, legal aid and nonprofits facing expensive research tools, with some relevance to higher education. She reports a $75 monthly price and attributes affordability to how the product is built. She also suggests larger firms might use an AI-native tool alongside established systems, but presents this as a market possibility rather than documented adoption.
qs: And we're charging $75 a month, so we're definitely in a different space.
we're very focused on the solo and small because they're the ones who need us the most.

But we also believe that mid and big also would be interested in looking at what we're doing because even if they have the big established tools, those tools have AI built on top of legacy systems which creates its own problems.

kp.k: Market entry need not displace incumbent research platforms
kp.d: Peterson rejects dethroning Westlaw as a realistic startup strategy and instead advocates creating a category between free search and premium research tools. The founders report being compared with Casetext and Fastcase before acquisition and describe demand from lawyers whose occasional research needs do not justify $500 monthly expenditure. These are positioning claims and customer observations, not market-share evidence.
qs: The only way to win here is not somehow dethroning the big ones.
there's so much room between Google Scholar and co-counsel.
We get lawyers who maybe need to do legal research once or twice a month, and it doesn't justify $500 a month.

kp.k: User needs drive progression from retrieval to research synthesis
kp.d: The founders describe moving from plain-language concept search, citation and case-name search, keywords and issue mapping toward a question-answering tool. Users wanted both treatment information and actionable synthesis, prompting an AI citator described as patent pending and capable of issue-level citation, followed by the newer research workflow. The transcript does not supply independent accuracy evidence for the citator.
qs: we mapped all the legal issues of every single opinion so you could see what cases address what issues.
One of the first things we did was build AI citator, which is now patent pending because it does issue level citation, which is pretty cool.
But it's not wrapping it up with a bow and giving me a and now what type thing. That's what the new tool does.

kp.k: Clarification and coverage checks precede corpus-grounded answers
kp.d: DiBona says the newer workflow first clarifies the question, including jurisdiction and party position, then checks whether the database covers the issue before researching. He contrasts this with general models filling in missing information. Host Chad Main provides a concrete usage example: the tool asked him to identify a missing California statutory section. The reported design grounds answers in Descrybe's 100 million row legal database rather than model knowledge alone.
qs: The first step is actually go through this question and make sure you have everything you need to do this research.
Then it'll go off and check and see if we have the coverage.
It's actually answering based on the law that is in our 100 million row database.
It prompted me and said, hey, what section are you talking about?

kp.k: Primary-law acquisition creates costs and strategic differentiation
kp.d: The founders report coverage of all state appellate and supreme courts, federal appellate and supreme courts, much federal district case law, all federal statutes and regulations, and statutes and regulations for approximately the 10 largest states. They describe ongoing direct collection as difficult, particularly from state websites, but preferable to expensive licensing and dependency on another company. Their claimed competitive advantage lies in assembling and cleaning the corpus.
qs: So we have all state appellate and supreme, and we have federal appellate and supreme and a lot of federal district.
And then for statutes and regs, we have I think like the top 10 biggest, largest states. We have all federal statutes and regs and we're growing every day.
And you possibly could license it from someone, but it would be so expensive. And then you're relying on another company for your data.

kp.k: Data preparation underpins the founders' reliability argument
kp.d: DiBona attributes performance to collecting, structuring, cleaning and storing legal data over three years since 2023 rather than concentrating initially on chatbots. The founders report using 100 billion tokens, subsequently qualifying the total as somewhere between that and a trillion, for data preparation rather than client work. Peterson argues that shortcuts in complex system construction can introduce foundational defects that surface in outputs; these are vendor explanations, not independently established causal findings.
qs: We just spent years, those three years since 2023.
We were just collecting and structuring data and going through and cleaning up the data and storing the data, which is my background.
100 billion with the B tokens
none of it was spent on client work, it was spent curating, cleaning, restructuring the data.
It's probably more than that. The next level was a trillion. Wow. So we're somewhere in between.

kp.k: Legal librarians contribute product testing and feedback
kp.d: Peterson says attorneys advise the nonlawyer founders and identifies legal librarians as especially important reviewers of research tools. She treats librarian approval as a demanding quality threshold while emphasizing continued pressure testing. A partnership and curriculum involvement are discussed prospectively, not as established educational outcomes.
qs: we have great attorneys advising us, we're not trying to figure this out on our own.
One of the best decisions early on was that the type of people we wanted to rely on were legal librarians.
But you always have to pressure test this stuff.

kp.k: Vendor benchmarking examines reasoning beyond answer accuracy
kp.d: Peterson describes a self-conducted white-paper comparison against foundation models, not competing legal tools, using MBE-style questions with answer keys to avoid commissioning costly bespoke lawyer assessment. Models had to explain both their selected answer and rejection of alternatives. She reports a larger-than-expected performance gap favoring Descrybe and confidently wrong reasoning from general models. The transcript supplies no sample size, numerical results, full model specifications or grading protocol; Peterson acknowledges self-testing limitations and that multiple-choice performance is only a proxy for legal reasoning.
qs: this is why we only tested against foundation models and not other legal tech tools
That's why we did the MBE style questions.
not only did you get the right letter, but did you reason to it correctly?
It's like, well, oh, gee, you tested yourself and you did well. What a shock, you know, I get it.
Obviously, nobody's practicing the law with multiple choice questions.

kp.k: Internal testing attributes answer differences to corpus grounding
kp.d: DiBona reports a separate unpublished comparison in which the new tool's access to Descrybe data was switched off and answers based on model knowledge were compared with corpus-grounded answers through a similar interface. He describes a measurable difference assessed using rubrics, without giving numerical results. Peterson extends this into a hypothesis that purpose-built tools referencing cleaned, vetted legal data should deliver more authoritative answers, including tools other than Descrybe.
qs: we turned that off and said, just use your own knowledge to get the answers.
And it was actually measurably different.
We didn't publish that as a white paper or anything.
We do think it's a category-wide thing

kp.k: Confident errors and opaque markets complicate tool selection
kp.d: Peterson warns that persuasive but incorrect legal reasoning is difficult for practitioners to distinguish from reliable output and can have serious consequences. She also recounts legal-aid buyers and venture capitalists independently saying they could not differentiate legal-tech products. Her recommendation is more transparent benchmarking and better metrics so buyers can judge tools on quality rather than marketing visibility; the reported buyer difficulties are anecdotal.
qs: So it would be very convincingly telling you why this was the right answer.
it's very hard to separate the truth from the fiction. And there's some big consequences for people on that.
we know we need solutions, but we can't tell the difference between all these tools.
we need to give better metrics to the market so they can make good decisions.

kp.k: Foundation-model competition remains an acknowledged strategic uncertainty
kp.d: Asked whether large model companies could eventually absorb specialist legal functionality, Peterson says dismissing the threat would be naive. She questions whether those companies will enter every specific domain and suggests collaboration or partnership as possible alternatives. These are strategic possibilities, not predictions supported by adoption or investment data.
qs: They're either lying or dangerously naive. Because obviously, we all have to think about that.
what makes sense for these companies to try to get into every little specific domain? Maybe not.
Maybe there's models where it's more of like a collaboration or partnership or things of that nature.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Peterson and DiBona claim AI-native legal research can make useful legal information and tools affordable to underserved users without displacing the major incumbents.
pts.d: Peterson links the product to their own difficulty understanding case law and to access to justice for people with fewer resources. She says the company's architecture allows it to offer advanced tools for a fraction of legacy-tool prices, quoting $75 per month. Its principal commercial audience is solo and small firms, with legal aid, nonprofits and higher education also facing affordability constraints. Larger firms might use an AI-native tool alongside existing subscriptions. Peterson explicitly rejects dethroning Westlaw as the strategy; DiBona identifies occasional researchers as a viable underserved market. These are claims about affordability and market positioning, not demonstrated reductions in unmet legal need.

pts.k: DiBona and Peterson describe AI research moving beyond case retrieval toward clarified questions, issue-level treatment and synthesized answers grounded in primary law.
pts.d: DiBona describes a workflow that first asks for missing information, such as jurisdiction or party position, then checks corpus coverage before researching. He says testing showed better results when the system established what it should research first. Peterson describes an AI citator, reported as patent pending, that supplies issue-level citation treatment, followed by a newer tool intended to give users a more actionable synthesis. Their claim concerns a purpose-built research workflow; they do not establish autonomous legal practice or elimination of human checking.

pts.k: Peterson and DiBona claim curated legal data materially improves answer authority and reasoning compared with general-purpose models, which can produce convincingly wrong answers.
pts.d: Peterson attributes the claimed advantage to tools referencing cleaned, vetted and structured legal data rather than relying on general model knowledge and heterogeneous sources. She reports a larger-than-expected performance gap in their own comparison and warns that confidently wrong explanations make general models risky for practicing attorneys. She extrapolates the advantage to other purpose-built legal tools, and potentially medical and scientific tools, while acknowledging that other legal products were not tested. DiBona similarly attributes performance to their corpus and years of data preparation. The transcript does not provide numerical comparative scores.

pts.k: DiBona claims AI substantially amplifies experienced developers' productivity, enabling a very small legal-tech vendor to build sophisticated tools.
pts.d: DiBona estimates that AI lets him accomplish the equivalent of ten programmers' work by coordinating multiple machines. Peterson presents their two-person, unfunded company as an example of AI empowering small teams whose founders already cover engineering and marketing. The productivity estimate is his experience-based claim, not a measured staffing comparison. They also identify limits: growth requires additional support, and they deliberately retain personal customer service rather than hand it over entirely to AI. This concerns legal-tech production, not a prediction that ten lawyers can be replaced.

pts.k: Peterson argues that proprietary data preparation and robust systems differentiate legal-AI products, while future competition from foundation-model companies remains uncertain.
pts.d: Peterson says independently assembling primary law avoids costly licensing and reliance on another company. Both founders describe years of collecting, cleaning and structuring data, with more than 100 billion tokens reportedly used for that preparation rather than client work. Peterson warns that inadequately engineered wrappers or vibe-coded systems can contain underlying defects. Asked about foundation-model encroachment, she treats it as a genuine risk but offers specialization, collaboration or partnership as possible outcomes, not a firm prediction that legal-tech vendors will remain protected.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main comparative evidence is founder-run testing using MBE-style questions and an unpublished comparison with corpus access disabled.
pts.d: Peterson says their white paper compared Descrybe with foundation models, not competing legal research products. MBE-style questions supplied an answer key; models were asked to explain their choice and rejection of alternatives so the exercise could assess reasoning as well as answer selection. She calls this a proxy for legal reasoning and acknowledges the caveat of testing one's own product. DiBona reports a separate internal test comparing the same interface using model knowledge alone with its corpus-grounded version; Peterson applied rubrics, but that comparison was not published. The transcript supplies no sample size, model versions, numerical scores, detailed scoring protocol or independent replication.

pts.k: Other support consists of founder experience, user feedback, reported operational scale and consultation with legal librarians and attorneys.
pts.d: The access rationale rests on the founders' employment-related research experience and their inference that people with less privilege face greater barriers. Product development is described as responsive to users seeking citation treatment and fuller answers. Peterson says attorneys advise them and legal librarians review the tools. Corpus size, token usage, pricing and developer productivity are self-reported. These support the founders' account of product development but are not presented as measured access-to-justice outcomes or independent proof of product-wide reliability. Peterson's argument for clearer market metrics also draws on conversations about difficulty distinguishing legal-tech products.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern the product and model landscape at the 2026 interview; advantages depend on expertise, data quality and available legal coverage.
pts.d: The founders date their motivating legal issue to approximately 2021 and the free-search launch to July 2023, describing roughly three subsequent years of data preparation. DiBona reports coverage of state appellate and supreme courts, federal appellate and Supreme Court decisions, substantial federal district material, all federal statutes and regulations, and statutes and regulations for approximately the ten largest states, with expansion ongoing. The workflow checks coverage before proceeding. Peterson qualifies criticism of general models as applying to how they are built 'right now.' The claimed developer amplification assumes an already skilled engineer. No definite forecast date is given for foundation-model competition, partnerships or incumbent displacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span public access, small-practice affordability, lawyer reliance risks, legal-tech competition and vendor staffing.
pts.d: Individuals confronting unfamiliar legal problems are the access-to-justice beneficiaries envisaged by the founders, especially those less privileged than themselves. Solo and small firms, legal aid organizations, nonprofits, higher education and occasional researchers are identified as users priced out of stronger tools. Mid-sized and large firms are possible supplementary buyers rather than necessarily replacement customers. Practicing attorneys and their clients face the consequences of misleading general-model answers. Legal librarians contribute product scrutiny. Small legal-tech vendors benefit from AI-assisted engineering but still need human operational support; incumbent research providers and foundation-model companies form the competitive context.
